content.text: Mass and weight are often confused in everyday language, but in physics they are two distinct concepts. Understanding the difference is essential for solving problems involving forces and gravity.
In everyday language, people say 'I weigh 70 kg', but in physics, mass is measured in kg and weight is measured in newtons (N). Weight is a force caused by gravity acting on mass.

Astronauts in orbit feel "weightless" even though gravity is still acting on them. This is because:
They are in free fall around Earth
The spacecraft falls at the same rate as they do
There is no reaction force pushing up on them
Their mass and weight are still present—they just don't feel the weight.
What you feel (can be zero in free fall)

Spring scales show weight but are calibrated for Earth
Weight is NOT measured in kilograms. Kilograms measure mass. Weight is a force and must be given in newtons. Using W = mg, a 60 kg person on Earth weighs 60 x 9.8 = 588 N.
"Mass and weight are the same thing"
— Mass is amount of matter (kg); weight is gravitational force (N).
— Incorrect! Your mass is 70 kg; your weight is about 700 N on Earth.
— They still have weight (gravity acts even in orbit). They experience apparent weightlessness because they're in free fall.
— Without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass.
— The value of g varies with location. 10 m/s² is an approximation for Earth's surface.
— Kitchen and bathroom scales show mass (kg) but actually measure weight and convert it assuming Earth's g value.
